item.title: Resource-Tunable Quantum Circuit Implementation of Nonlinear Element-Wise Transformations
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Circuit depth for entry-wise Hadamard matrix polynomial transformations of degree 2d−1 reduced to 𝒪(n+d) via polynomial factorization into m parallel factors, matching the query lower bound of 2d−1 single-oracle queries when m=2d−1.

Grade 0.478 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for…” · Chunlin Yang, Yuqi Li, Hongmei Yao, Zhaobing Fan

Figure

Circuit architecture decomposing a Hadamard matrix function into m low-degree factors P(s)(A) combined via a parallel quantum Hadamard product.

Asks

Can the circuit depth for implementing a Hadamard matrix function on block-encoded data be reduced below linear in the polynomial degree?

Before

Linear circuit depth in the polynomial degree with logarithmic auxiliary space (Kao et al. 2024 / Ref. [19]).

But

Entries of input matrix must lie on compact domain Ω⊆ℂ with connected complement ℂ∖Ω; relies on post-selection with success probability scaling inversely with the square of the normalization factor α.

Tools

Polynomial factorization · Block encoding · Quantum Hadamard product (QHP) · Binary-tree recursion

Code. https://github.com/ChunlinYANG0/QuantumHadamardProcedure

Abstract

Nonlinear transformations are important in quantum machine learning and other quantum numerical applications, which can be reduced to the implementation of element-wise polynomials through polynomial approximation. Existing works establish the feasibility of transformations and improve query or auxiliary-space efficiency, but circuit depth remains linear in scale with degree. In this work, we develop a resource-tunable quantum framework that decomposes a (2^d-1)-degree polynomial into m lower-degree factors, with m controlling the degree of parallelism. By varying m from 1 to 2^d-1, the framework provides a trade-off among query complexity, additional gate complexity, ancilla count, and normalization, ranging from a binary-tree implementation to a O(n+d)-depth construction with highly parallel oracle queries that match the query lower bound. The effects of polynomial approximation and implementation errors are further analyzed. We demonstrate the framework for nonlinear activation functions such as sigmoid and tanh, as well as pixel-wise image transformations.

item.title: Transducer-based linear combination of unitaries: theory and applications
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Transducer-based linear combination of unitaries implements block-encoding of A/α with rescaling α=𝒪(a) using 𝒪(Cmax⁡log⁡(1/ϵ)+(λ/a)C(log⁡(1/ϵ))2) primitive queries. Converts transducer action to ϵ-approximate block-encoding in 𝒪(Klog⁡(1/ϵ)) queries via resolvent norm K.

Grade 0.468 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for…” · Dong An, Dekuan Dong, Changpeng Shao, Yuxin Zhang, Chenhao Zhao

Asks

Can quantum coherence be preserved in linear combinations of unitaries while reducing query complexity from worst-case to weighted-average cost?

Before

Standard LCU with amplitude amplification required 𝒪~(Cmax⁡λ/a) queries (Gilyén et al. 2019).

But

Requires constituent unitaries to access a common family of primitive oracles coherently, and requires an a priori upper bound a≥‖A‖.

Tools

transducer framework · resolvent norm analysis · Cayley transformation · finite-reuse catalyst removal · tunable variable-time amplitude amplification

Abstract

Linear combination of unitaries (LCU) is a fundamental primitive in quantum algorithms, whose cost is typically governed by the most expensive unitary appearing in the combination. We develop a transducer-based LCU framework that reduces this worst-case dependence to a weighted average query complexity, when the constituent unitaries share access to a common set of primitive oracles. Consider A=∑_j c_j U_j, where c_j>0 and each unitary U_j can be implemented using C_j primitive queries. Given an upper bound a≥|A|, our algorithm implements a block-encoding of A/α with rescaling factor α=O(a), using widetildeO (C_max+overlineC λ/a ) primitive queries, where λ=∑_j c_j, C_max=max_j C_j, and overlineC= ∑_j c_j C_j/λ. By comparison, the standard LCU construction requires widetildeO (C_max λ/a ) primitive queries. The improvement can therefore be substantial when costly unitaries have small weights and λ/a is large. As applications, we obtain improved block-encodings of sparse matrices, leading to quantum algorithms for sparse Hamiltonian simulation and quantum linear systems with near-optimal query complexity up to polylogarithmic factors in all relevant parameters. Our main technique is the transducer framework developed by Belovs, Jeffery, and Yolcu [Quantum, 8:1444 (2024)]. Here we develop a complementary operator-level theory tailored to block-encodings. We identify the resolvent norm K as a key complexity measure for transducer implementation besides the existing catalyst complexity. We show that the transducer action can be converted into an ε-approximate block-encoding using only O(K log(1/ε)) queries to the transducer, improving the precision dependence from polynomial to logarithmic.

item.title: Shadow Quantum Singular Value Transformation with Shallow Quantum Circuits
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Observable estimation ⟨ψ|f(H)†Ojf(H)|ψ⟩ with QSVT achieves quantum circuit depth O(rDH) or O(sDH), where r is the H-invariant Krylov dimension, s≤r is the observable-visible Krylov dimension, and DH is the block-encoding depth of H.

Grade 0.454 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for…” · Nai-Hui Chia, Hyunseong Kim, Chia-Ying Lin

Asks

Can we use the QSVT framework to enable end-to-end quantum applications within the coherent circuit depth constraints of early fault-tolerant quantum computers?

Before

Standard QSVT circuit depth scales linearly with polynomial degree deg⁡(f) independent of state or observable structure.

But

Requires H-invariance or accurate low-dimensional truncation of the Krylov subspace 𝒦r(H,|ψ⟩), bounded polynomial norm ratios, and well-conditioned Gram/shadow matrices.

Tools

Krylov subspace methods · Observable-aware quotient spaces · History-state constructions · Classical shadows · Hadamard test

Abstract

We introduce shadow quantum singular value transformation (Shadow QSVT): given an initial state |ψ⟩, a Hermitian matrix H, a polynomial f, and a set of observables O₁,…,O_m, the goal is to estimate ⟨ψ|f(H)^†O_j f(H)|ψ⟩ for all j∈1,…,m. Shadow QSVT provides a systematic route to reduce the quantum resources required by standard QSVT, which constructs a unitary block-encoding of f(H). It uses structure in the input state and observables, together with the fact that many applications require only observable estimates rather than synthesizing the full unitary. We present three algorithms that exploit structure in the initial state and observables to reduce quantum circuit depth. First, we develop a state-aware QSVT algorithm that prepares the target state with low circuit depth when the Krylov subspace associated with H and |ψ⟩ is low-dimensional or admits an accurate low-dimensional approximation. Second, we introduce an observable-aware Shadow QSVT algorithm that combines a new observable-aware Krylov subspace with history states to further reduce circuit depth and gate complexity. Finally, we develop Classical Shadow QSVT, which constructs a classical representation from H, f, and |ψ⟩ without prior knowledge of the observables or explicit preparation of the target state proportional to f(H)|ψ⟩. This representation enables estimation of the target quantities for observables specified after the quantum computation. Together, these three algorithms provide tools for reducing the circuit depth of QSVT-based computations across a range of settings.

item.title: A physical and universal model of bosonic computations with Solovay-Kitaev theorem
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Bosonic Energy-Preserving Quantum Computation (BEQC) model uses energy-conserving gates driven by coherent state ancillae, efficiently simulating polynomial-energy continuous-variable circuits while recovering 𝖡𝖰𝖯 and enabling Solovay-Kitaev gate compilation.

Grade 0.443 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Dorian Rudolph, Arsalan Motamedi, Dhruva Sambrani, Hamid Reza Naeij, Ulysse Chabaud, Sevag Gharibian, Saeed Mehraban

Figure

Schematic of the BEQC architecture: vacuum state inputs alongside a coherent-state energy reservoir undergo a sequence of energy-preserving unitaries before final photon-number measurement.

Asks

How can continuous-variable quantum computation be formulated to prevent unphysical energy blowups and restore universal compilation?

Before

Standard Lloyd-Braunstein continuous-variable models allow doubly exponential energy growth in time t, diverging photon numbers, and lack general Solovay-Kitaev compilation guarantees.

But

Simulations of active non-energy-preserving operations require coherent ancilla amplitude α to scale with target precision O(1/ε); computational equivalence to 𝖡𝖰𝖯 holds specifically in the polynomial-energy regime.

Tools

Coherent state ancillae · Energy-preserving Hamiltonians · Linear optics and Kerr non-linearities · Lie-Trotter product formulas · Fock space truncation

Abstract

Bosonic quantum systems are among the leading architectures for quantum information processing, offering continuous-variable degrees of freedom with strong error-correction capabilities. However, standard bosonic quantum computation models such as the Lloyd-Braunstein [Lloyd and Braunstein, 1999] and hybrid oscillator-qubit models [Brenner, Dias, and Koenig, 2025; Liu et al., 2026] permit dramatic energy growth, leading to unphysical computational power and the breakdown of fundamental algorithmic tools such as universal and efficient compilation [Brenner et al., 2026; Rudolph et al., 2025]. To address this, we introduce a new model of bosonic quantum computation, Bosonic Energy-Preserving Quantum Computation (BEQC), in which energy is treated as a computational resource. Namely, energy is supplied solely through input coherent states, and all gates are generated by energy-preserving Hamiltonians. Thus, by construction, dramatic energy growth is impossible, making the model physically grounded. We next show that BEQC is a computationally robust and universal model in many respects, including: (1. Computational power) BEQC efficiently simulates all polynomial-energy computations in existing models, and exactly recovers BQP in the polynomial energy setting. It further admits several complexity-theoretic upper bounds when varying the energy, precision, and space parameters of the model. (2. Universal gate sets and state synthesis) BEQC has natural universal gate sets based on linear optics and Kerr interactions. In particular, we obtain a Solovay-Kitaev theorem which circumvents previous no-go results. We give various applications, including (a) a protocol for engineering GKP states with rigorous preparation guarantees, (b) Fock state preparation to exponential precision, and (c) native Fock space simulation of any qubit-based unitary.

item.title: A Quantum Scaling Algorithm for Maximum-Weight Perfect Matching in General Graphs
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Quantum algorithm computes exact maximum-weight perfect matching on general graphs with integer weights up to W in O~(nm2/3log⁡W) time.

Grade 0.439 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds” · Kourosh Mirsohi, Sandy Irani, Michael T. Goodrich

Figure

Schematic of an alternating augmenting path across contracted blossom roots ⟨B1,…,Br⟩, showing original-graph endpoints (ui,vi) and matched edges.

Asks

Can quantum algorithms achieve an asymptotic speedup over the best classical combinatorial algorithm for maximum-weight perfect matching on general graphs?

Before

Best classical combinatorial bound was O~(mnlog⁡W) (Duan, Pettie, and Su 2018); this improves it in the dense regime m≥n3/2.

But

Asymptotic time bound in the dense regime m≥n3/2 under QRAM model with unit-time coherent reads.

Tools

QRAM model with BBHT Grover search · Primal-dual weight scaling framework · Edmonds blossom contraction and laminar families · Liquidationist matching architecture

Abstract

Quantum speed-ups have been obtained for many fundamental graph problems, including most variants of matching. A notable exception, however, is the maximum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) problem in general graphs with integer edge weights, which is arguably the most challenging variant of matching. We present a quantum algorithm for MWPM in general graphs that runs in \( widetildeO(n m^2/3log W) \) time, where W is an upper bound on the magnitude of the edge weights. This is an improvement over the best known classical combinatorial bound of \( widetildeO(m√ n log W) \) in the dense regime, where m≥n^(3/2). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first quantum algorithm to obtain an asymptotic improvement over the best classical combinatorial algorithm for the MWPM problem in general graphs. The running time of our method accounts for QRAM initialization and access overheads up to polylogarithmic factors, as well as all classical updates to the data structures. At a high level, our algorithm is based on a classical framework due to Duan, Pettie, and Su, but our algorithm requires replacing certain classical tasks with quantum methods, alternative analysis of classical procedures, and the use of alternative data structures that can be implemented effectively in the QRAM model.

item.title: Reducing the Entanglement Cost of Distributed Bipartite Quantum Computation with Constant Qubit Overhead
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Every bipartite Clifford unitary is implementable via exact deterministic LOCC at the optimal entanglement lower bound ⌈log2⁡OpSch⁡(U)⌉ Bell pairs using at most two auxiliary qubits per QPU. Non-Clifford unitaries with Clifford+T decompositions require at most 2t additional Bell pairs, where t is the T-count.

Grade 0.426 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for…” · Kosuke Matsui, Jun-Yi Wu, Min-Hsiu Hsieh, Mio Murao

Figure

Decomposition of a 4-qubit Clifford unitary into three elementary blocks (G1,G2,G3) executed sequentially to achieve optimal entanglement consumption.

Asks

Can the operator Schmidt rank lower bound on entanglement cost for distributed bipartite unitaries be achieved with constant auxiliary qubit overhead per QPU?

Before

was (2nA,2nB) auxiliary qubits for Choi-state teleportation attaining log2⁡OpSch⁡(U) Bell pairs (Eisert et al. 2000, Zhou et al. 2000)

But

Deterministic exact LOCC with perfect shared Bell pairs; bipartite setting with at most two QPUs.

Tools

operator Schmidt rank decomposition · symplectic matrix factorization · elementary block decomposition · mid-circuit measurement and qubit reuse

Abstract

Distributed quantum computation connects multiple quantum processing units (QPUs) through quantum communication to jointly perform large-scale quantum computations. Since the number of qubits available at each QPU is limited, it is important to reduce quantum communication while keeping the qubit overhead small. To this end, we study an entanglement-assisted model, in which entanglement consumption serves as a measure of quantum communication cost. item.title: A Noise Operator Approach to Quantum Query Complexity and Time-Space Tradeoff Lower Bounds
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Proves fully general quantum query lower bound of Ω(n4/3(log⁡log⁡n)/(S1/3log⁡n)) for sorting n numbers from [n2] using at most S qubits, and Ω(nm/S) queries for computing almost all hash functions from strongly universal families mapping n bits to m bits.

Grade 0.426 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds” · Paul Beame, Blake Holman, Niels Kornerup

Asks

Can unconditional time-space tradeoff lower bounds be proven for general (adaptive, non-output-oblivious) quantum sorting algorithms and universal hash families?

Before

Only output-oblivious sorting bounds were known: T=Ω(n3/2/S) (Klauck, Špalek, de Wolf 2003). For integer multiplication, prior quantum bound was Ω(n2/(Slog⁡n)) (Beame, Kornerup, Whitmeyer 2024).

But

Asymptotic regime for large n. Inputs drawn uniformly from [n2] for sorting and Dn for linear algebra problems. S≤cg/17 for $(g, h, c)$-rigid matrix products.

Tools

Noise operator method · Recording-query basis (compressed oracle) · Quantum noise stability bounds · Matrix rigidity analysis

Abstract

Time and space (memory) are two of the most important measures of cost in computation, even more so for quantum computation. In quantum computation our tools for proving unconditional tradeoffs between time and space are surprisingly limited. The first quantum time-space tradeoff lower bounds were proven for sorting by Klauck, Špalek and de Wolf. Unfortunately, their method is limited to proving output-oblivious lower bounds (i.e. the lower bounds only apply to algorithms with a non-adaptive output schedule) and other methods have yielded nothing beyond output-oblivious lower bounds for sorting.We prove the first fully general quantum time-space tradeoff lower bound for sorting. We do so by introducing a novel method based on the noise operator to add to the analysis toolkit for proving quantum query and time space tradeoff lower bounds. By combining our resulting quantum noise stability bound with quantum recording query methods, we prove an Ω(n^(4/3) (loglogn)/(S^(1/3) logn)) lower bound on the number of queries that a fully general quantum algorithm with at most S qubits of memory requires to sort n numbers from [n²]. Applying our noise operator argument involves purely classical arguments, which makes it particularly simple to use. We also us it to prove that, for any strongly universal (pairwise independent) hash function family H from n bits to m bits, almost all hash functions in H require a quantum algorithm with at most S qubits of memory to make Ω(nm/S) queries to an input x in order to compute h(x), even with very small success probability. Previously, Mansour, Nisan, and Tiwari had shown a similar classical lower bound using their hash mixing lemma. Our noise operator method allows us to use a related but simpler property of hash functions to prove our lower bounds.

item.title: Verifiable Quantum Advantage and Computation via Quantum Circuit Obfuscation
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Two-message, publicly and classically verifiable quantum-advantage protocol constructed from quantum indistinguishability obfuscation (qiO) for ancilla-free unitaries assuming 𝖡𝖰𝖯⊈i.o.𝖡𝖯𝖯.

Grade 0.423 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “sampling-based quantum advantage and its classical spoofing” · Alexandru Gheorghiu, Aparna Gupte, Vojtvech Havlívcek, Yunchao Liu

Figure

Implication graph showing how quantum RIO, SCP, and qiO for ancilla-free and tidy circuits lead to private and public classical verification of 𝖡𝖰𝖯 computations and verifiable quantum advantage.

Asks

Can the security of peaked-circuit quantum advantage and classical verification of 𝖡𝖰𝖯 be based on cryptographic quantum indistinguishability obfuscation?

But

Requires quantum indistinguishability obfuscation for ancilla-free unitaries, 𝖡𝖰𝖯⊈i.o.𝖡𝖯𝖯, and post-quantum one-way functions for public verification of 𝖡𝖰𝖯.

Tools

quantum indistinguishability obfuscation · peaked random circuit sampling · worst-to-average-case reduction via local mixing · ancilla-free tidy circuit compilation

Abstract

We construct protocols for classically verifiable quantum advantage and classical verification of BQP computations using emphquantum indistinguishability obfuscation (qiO). Specifically, given qiO and assuming a slightly stronger version of BQP≠BPP, we construct a two-message quantum-advantage protocol that is efficiently and publicly verifiable. Our result can be viewed as a rigorous cryptographic foundation for the heuristic quantum advantage proposals based on emphpeaked random circuit sampling of Aaronson and Zhang (arXiv:2404.14493). We also construct two simple protocols for classically verifying arbitrary BQP computations. The first protocol is privately verifiable and assumes only the existence of qiO. This gives a rare example of a nontrivial cryptographic application of (quantum) iO that does not make additional computational hardness assumptions. The second protocol additionally assumes post-quantum one-way functions and is emphpublicly verifiable. To our knowledge, this is the first publicly verifiable protocol for classical verification of BQP computations under computational assumptions in the standard model. We show that all our results hold when qiO is assumed only for ancilla-free unitary circuits. As evidence supporting this assumption, we prove a worst-to-average-case reduction for obfuscating such circuits. This reduction extends the local-mixing framework of Canetti, Chamon, Mucciolo and Ruckenstein (TCC 2024) under quantum analogues of their assumptions.
